units.label: 实验2：说出或沉默
units.description: 同一候选话语二元反应，目标×CoT；继承人类材料但不同反应量尺。

units.label: 实验3：住房和餐饮迁移
units.description: GPT系列在两语境复用二元协议及三种目标；不把各模型作为新实验。

units.label: 共享signaling bandits与RSA
units.description: 可计算世界、听者更新、效用权衡及统计拟合；为三实验服务，不自行训练LLM。

units.label: 既有人类参照与定性轨迹
units.description: 人类既有数据及示例轨迹辅助理解，不是新增人类或独立模型行为实验。

facts.statement: 研究LLM在交流中如何权衡honesty与helpfulness，以受控signaling bandits把真但无用和假但有用的信息分开；提供的世界状态定义truthfulness，不直接观察模型实际信念。

method_function.text: 将交际价值转化为可区分的输出及潜在效用。

facts.statement: 蘑菇有颜色与纹理两组各3特征，效用为两个特征分数相加；每轮向不知道奖励的游客提供3个选项，只允许一条特征—数值消息，材料使真实度与帮助收益可分离。

method_function.text: 构造可计算真值和听者决策收益的微型世界。

facts.statement: 实验1让模型生成一句话，6个特征乘5个取值[-2,-1,0,1,2]形成30种可能话语；30条候选并非完整列在上下文供选择；比较默认与CoT及7种现成模型。

method_function.text: 测量受约束的自由消息选择。

facts.statement: 实验2给定一条话语，模型二选一决定说出或保持沉默，沉默对应听者随机选择；使用中性、诚实、有用三种目标和默认/CoT条件；继承人类材料，但人类滑尺改为模型重复二元反应。

method_function.text: 以相同候选信息考察真值与帮助收益冲突下的认可。

facts.statement: 实验3把实验2改为住房和餐饮，两类场景保持特征数、选项数、数值结构，选择无固有偏好排序的特征；仅测试GPT系列。

method_function.text: 检验相同决策结构在语境更换后的稳健性。

facts.statement: 现成GPT3.5/GPT4/GPT4Turbo、Llama2 70B/base与chat、Mixtral8x7B/base与instruct比较；Llama temperature .1/top_p .9，Mixtral .7/1，GPT1/1。现成前后RLHF版本比较不等于本文自行微调。

method_function.text: 区分模型条件与采样设置。

facts.statement: 每trial生成30次响应；默认回答20 token上限，CoT500。CoT要求先Reasoning再最终答案；实验1附录最终标签Message而正文统一写Answer。

method_function.text: 规定重复采样与思维链/最终反应分离协议。

facts.statement: 较弱/非chat模型为提高有效格式，使用同系列chat模型最常见的起始词作前缀；非chat将system与user以换行合并；附录阈值为parse accuracy<.4，并给Llama前缀例。

method_function.text: 处理不同接口和格式遵循能力。

facts.statement: 诚实/有用目标以system职责说明操纵：有用条件允许说假话，诚实条件要求真话；住房加入失去执照后果，餐饮加入对厨师无礼理由；住房/餐饮初始解析率高而未做额外提示工程。

method_function.text: 实施目标引导并记录语境条件的附加含义。

facts.statement: 材料呈现前随机化两组特征对应分数幅度、组内特征赋值、特征呈现次序及数值升降序；实验3沿用随机化。

method_function.text: 降低固定特征偏好及显示顺序影响。

facts.statement: 实验1正则解析，必须恰好一个特征及一个数值，否则剔除；报告解析率，真话比例、有用比例、平均帮助及假话中有用比例。

method_function.text: 从受约束文本编码消息并聚合行为指标。

facts.statement: 实验2/3用手工类别规则解析说出/沉默，CoT仅解析最终答案；报告认可比例、truthful比例、positive utility比例与mean reward lift；正文没有给完整规则表及这些指标的全部条件分母。

method_function.text: 从二元选择汇总认可及收益。

facts.statement: RSA诚实效用按话语在真实世界是否成立给+1或-1；speaker按exp(beta_S U) softmax抽取，beta_S控制最优化程度。

method_function.text: 从真值到效用再到概率选择的计算建模。

facts.statement: literal listener先按真值相容指示与均匀世界先验形成后验，排除不相容世界；对后验世界求期望奖励，再按beta_L softmax形成动作策略。

method_function.text: 定义接收信息后的信念更新和决策。

facts.statement: Eq6 helpfulness是听者策略在真实奖励下的期望值，Eq7把它与诚实效用按lambda和1-lambda线性混合；lambda0只重真值，1只重有用。文字另以相对随机选择改善解释有用性。

method_function.text: 分离多目标效用并定义权衡参数。

facts.statement: 沿用Sumers的WebPPL RSA，用lambda[0,1]步长.05、beta_S/beta_L[1,10]步长1的网格推断，边缘化beta_L并报告lambda和beta_S后验均值。

method_function.text: 拟合心理解释参数而不更新LLM权重。

facts.statement: 实验1比较CoT/default共享lambda的零假设与lambda_CoT>lambda_default的有序替代假设，用边缘似然/Bayes factor；为组合空间放大改用lambda步.1、beta_S步1及beta_L=[1,3,5,7,9]的较粗网格。

method_function.text: 检验CoT是否使帮助权重增大的有方向模型比较。

facts.statement: Fig4把人类既有数据与GPT4Turbo蘑菇/住房二元结果按true/false、目标和帮助值作图；点为单次响应、线为非参数回归，文章未报告平滑算法/带宽。

method_function.text: 检查真值与帮助值对响应曲线的交互模式。

facts.statement: 人类比较来源为Sumers等既有signaling bandits研究，图1注明经许可复用；模型实验2以重复二元选择近似人类滑尺的认可率。

method_function.text: 使用已有行为参照并保留量尺差异。

facts.statement: 对GPT4及Turbo极少说假话，表2不报假话有用率；Llama实验2均一说出/沉默时部分估计留空，部分模型从图3参数展示剔除；空白不代表零效应。

method_function.text: 处理退化响应和稀疏条件指标的可解释性。

facts.statement: 作者报告较大模型能同时诚实有用，部分较小模型在CoT下更重帮助而真值下降；目标提示和语境会改变权衡，现成RLHF版本通常改善基本表现。

method_function.text: 保存作者对条件差异的概括，不把潜在效用归因当内在动机证明。

facts.statement: 附录D展示Llama/Mixtral/GPT默认或目标引导下的完整推理样例，含推理中算术错误以及主动认可不真实但有用信息的例子；未给系统人工编码频率或一致性。

method_function.text: 以定性轨迹辅助解释选择，不作为独立普遍性计数。

facts.statement: 论文提供系统/用户模板、关键采样、网格和结果表，但未完整报告独立材料/试次数、所有API快照日期、随机种子/会话隔离、二元解析全集、参数先验/似然和非参数回归配置。

method_function.text: 标明本地已供全文可重建程度与准确缺项。

facts.statement: 受控小世界依赖已给真实状态且无真实社会/身体背景，无法直接观测模型所信；作者区分honesty/truthfulness并讨论外推限制。

method_function.text: 限定构念解释范围。

LLM literature. Evans et al. (2021) define “honesty” as only
making claims that the AI believes to be true — in contrast
to “truthfulness,” which they define as only making claims
that are in fact true. The related notion of “supportedness”
is defined as claims that are supported by evidence (Glaese
et al., 2022; Menick et al., 2022; Komeili et al., 2022). We
adopt the Gricean Maxim of Quality as an intuitive measure
of honesty in conversational settings. Grice phrased this
maxim as: “Do not say what you believe to be false, or for
which you lack adequate evidence” (Grice, 1975, p. 46).
This is formalized by associating a positive scalar utility
with true utterances and a negative utility on false ones:

The signaling bandits paradigm. To determine how LLMs
weigh honesty and helpfulness, we need a setting that decouples these values. If we ask LLMs to choose from a
set of utterances (some true but unhelpful; others false but
helpful; and so on), we can determine whether honesty or
helpfulness best explains their choices.

Thus, in our experiments, “truthfulness” and “supportedness”
are synonymous and can easily be measured (false claims
are not supported; true claims are). In contrast, we cannot
claim to know what an LLM “believes.” However, in GPT-4
Turbo at least, empirical results (Fig. 4) and reasoning traces
(Appendix D3, D4) clearly suggest that the model correctly
endorses which statements are true or false based on the
provided information – i.e., it “believes” this ground-truth
information about the world state. Thus, we chose to use the
term “honesty” to describe our work: it is consistent with our
formal model (unlike “supportedness”) — and intuitively,
an agent makes tradeoffs with respect to what they believe
to be true (which argues against “truthfulness”). Similarly,
there are many alternative formalizations of helpfulness: for
example, the Question Under Discussion (Roberts, 2012)
assumes that discourse is oriented towards answering a particular question at any point in time. Helpfulness is thus
measured by how much an utterance reduces the listener’s
uncertainty with respect to that question. This is a narrower
definition of helpfulness which is subsumed by the decisiontheoretic measure used here (see discussion in Sumers et al.,
2023), but it may be closer in spirit to Askell et al. (2021).

To accomplish this, we use signaling bandits (Sumers et al.,
2021; 2023), a variant of Lewis signaling games (Lewis,
1969) which places the speaker and a listener in a contextual
bandit setting (Sutton & Barto, 2018). We follow the experiment structure of Sumers et al. (2023): the LLM acts as a
guide helping naı̈ve tourists forage for mushrooms. In each
trial, a new tourist who knows nothing about mushrooms
must choose one from a set of three mushrooms. The guide
is allowed to produce a single utterance to aid the tourist’s
choice. The guide’s utterance is honest if it is factually accurate (Eq. 2), and helpful if it increases the expected utility
of the listener’s policy over a random choice (Eq. 6).

Formally, mushrooms are characterized by binary features:

Trade-offs between helpfulness and honesty. While typical alignment benchmarks measure honesty and helpfulness
independently, everyday use requires trading off between
them. In pursuit of helpfulness, people readily approximate
the truth by rounding numerical values (Van Der Henst et al.,
2002; Krifka, 2007), tell white lies out of politeness (Wang,
2019; Yoon et al., 2020) and endorse false-but-helpful statements (van Rooij & Schulz, 2020; Tessler & Goodman,
2019). Formally, we model the trade-off between values by
defining the speaker’s utility function as a convex combination of helpfulness and honesty:

ϕ : A → {0, 1}K

so each mushroom may be red (or not); or have spots (or
not), and so on. Rewards R are linear over these features,
parameterized by a vector reward function w:
R(a, w) = w⊤ ϕ(a).

(9)

Figure 1A depicts this visually: each mushroom has a color
and a texture (its features ϕ, Eq. 8). Each feature has a scalar
reward determined by the reward vector (or world state) w.
Finally, the reward for choosing a mushroom is the sum of
the reward for each of its features (Eq. 9).

The speaker (in our case, a LLM) helps the listener by
producing a single utterance that is informative about the
reward function (Fig. 1B). Utterances are restricted to the
form “[Feature] is worth [value]”, e.g., “Spots are +1.” This
means that the speaker is allowed to provide information
about a single dimension of the reward vector w.
Crucially, not all truthful utterances are helpful, and vice
versa. For example, as shown in Figure 1C, “Red is 0” or
“Green is +2” are honest but not helpful: they do not improve
the listener’s policy. Other utterances are false but helpful:
“Red is +1” or “Spots are +2” are false, but improve the
listener’s policy (Eq. 6) by shifting it towards the optimal

Message:

Models and hyperparameters. For each experiment, we
investigate the communicative qualities of a collection of
state-of-the-art open- and closed-source models: GPT-3.5
Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo, LLaMa 2 70B chat, LLaMa
2 70B, Mixtral 8x7B instruct v0.1, and Mixtral 8x7B v0.1.
This includes two pairs of models before and after RLHF,
allowing us to investigate how RLHF influences model behavior. We use temperature = 0.1, top p = 0.9 for the LLaMa
models following (Touvron et al., 2023), temperature = 0.7,
top p = 1 for the Mixtral models following their API2 , and
temperature = 1, top p = 1 for the GPT models following
their API3 and Liu & Shah (2023).

Prompting. We prompt LLMs to act as a tour guide
following Sumers et al. (2023), and include instructions
on response formatting. We also prompt with and without
chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022). We performed prompt
engineering in weaker and non-chat models to encourage
valid responses. Specifically, we took the most common
phrase that started the responses of stronger models of the
same series (GPT, LLaMa, Mixtral) and appended them to
the prompt as an initial start to the response.

We first test the behaviors of LLMs when choosing from
a set of 30 possible utterances: 6 features in Figure 1A
and 5 values in [-2, -1, 0, +1, +2]. This setting represents
a relatively natural advice-giving interaction, albeit with
restricted and stylized semantics. It allows a direct comparison with human data from Sumers et al. (2023), and
tests whether LLMs select truthful and helpful information
when candidate responses are not provided in context and
multiple utterances are available.

and ask the LLM to choose between saying the utterance or
staying silent. Concretely, in the example shown in Fig. 1B,
we can ask the LLM whether it would be willing to say
“Red is +1.” This is false (red is 0) but helpful, as it draws
the listener away from the negative blue mushroom. Thus,
endorsing it suggests the LLM prioritizes helpfulness over
honesty. In contrast, in contexts with a blue spotted mushroom (where blue is -2 and spotted is +1, giving a net value
of -1), we can ask whether it would say “Spots are +1”.
This is true but not helpful, since it biases them towards a
negative mushroom.

We quantify the relevance of each {context, utterance} pair
based on the expected value of a listener’s choice (Eq. 6).
Each pair is also classified as either truthful or untruthful.
While the human version used a slider between the options
“say the utterance” and “stay silent”, we used a binary choice
due to concerns over LLMs’ ability to interpret the scale
and represent its own uncertainty over the numerical values. We sample multiple times and randomize features to
approximate a continuous ‘endorsement value.’ Prompts are
available in Appendix A.2.

6. Experiment 2: To say or not to say
Our first experiment evaluates how LLMs balance helpfulness and honesty when choosing from a range of utterances.
But when these are directly in conflict, which do models
prioritize? In this experiment, we ask whether LLMs are
willing to endorse options that satisfy one value while violating the other. We use utterance-context pairs from Sumers
et al. (2023) that put honesty and helpfulness in conflict,

Steerability. We also examine the effect of adding a prompt
that encourages either honesty or helpfulness. Humans
respond to these prompts by upweighting the relevant value;
we examine whether LLMs can apply a simple zero-shot
prompt to make similar trade-offs.
We find that pre-RLHF Mixtral and LLaMa models do not

Recognizing this parallel allows us to formalize these concepts via the Rational Speech Acts framework (RSA, Goodman & Frank, 2016; Frank & Goodman, 2012; Degen, 2023).
RSA views communication as a form of rational action (Simon, 1955). Speech is modeled as a choice from a set of
possible utterances: the speaker ascribes utilities to each
utterance and chooses one based on these utilities. The
utility of an utterance is denoted U (u, w), formalizing the
idea that the value of an utterance depends on the world
state. Returning to the example of telling the time (Van
Der Henst et al., 2002), we can imagine that if the true time
were 5:00pm, most speakers would place a high utility on
the utterance “It’s 5pm” and a low utility on the utterance
“It’s 6pm.” However, at 6:00pm, these preferences would be
reversed. We then assume that speakers choose an utterance
u via soft-max over this utility function:
PS (u | w) ∝ exp{ βS · U (u, w) },

where δJuK (w) denotes the meaning of u: it evaluates to 1
when u is consistent with the world w, and 0 otherwise.

δJ“It’s 6pm”K (5:00pm) = 0. Eq. 2 thus assigns a positive utility to true utterances and a negative utility to false ones.

We can then fit the free parameters βS , βL , and λ to LLM
responses. Our analysis focuses in particular on the λ parameter, which defines the trade-off between helpfulness
and honesty. When λ is 0, models care only about producing truthful utterances, while when λ is 1, models care only
about being helpful. Finally, intermediate values — characteristic of human communication — represent different
trade-offs between the two values.

The speaker (in our case, a LLM) helps the listener by
producing a single utterance that is informative about the
reward function (Fig. 1B). Utterances are restricted to the
form “[Feature] is worth [value]”, e.g., “Spots are +1.” This
means that the speaker is allowed to provide information
about a single dimension of the reward vector w.
Crucially, not all truthful utterances are helpful, and vice
versa. For example, as shown in Figure 1C, “Red is 0” or
“Green is +2” are honest but not helpful: they do not improve
the listener’s policy. Other utterances are false but helpful:
“Red is +1” or “Spots are +2” are false, but improve the
listener’s policy (Eq. 6) by shifting it towards the optimal

To accomplish this, we use signaling bandits (Sumers et al.,
2021; 2023), a variant of Lewis signaling games (Lewis,
1969) which places the speaker and a listener in a contextual
bandit setting (Sutton & Barto, 2018). We follow the experiment structure of Sumers et al. (2023): the LLM acts as a
guide helping naı̈ve tourists forage for mushrooms. In each
trial, a new tourist who knows nothing about mushrooms
must choose one from a set of three mushrooms. The guide
is allowed to produce a single utterance to aid the tourist’s
choice. The guide’s utterance is honest if it is factually accurate (Eq. 2), and helpful if it increases the expected utility
of the listener’s policy over a random choice (Eq. 6).

B. Psychological Model Details
Parameter inference. We use the WebPPL (Goodman & Stuhlmüller, 2014) model from Sumers et al. (2023), following
their procedure of a grid search to infer model parameters. We used the same grid of λ ∈ [0, 1] in steps of .05 and
βS , βL ∈ [1, 10] in steps of 1. We marginalize over βL and report the posterior mean for λ and βS in Tables 2, 3, and 4.

Chain of Thought versus Default prompting (Exp 1). Our hypothesis is that chain-of-thought prompting will bias models
towards helpfulness over honesty. Formally, this means that the λChain of Thought > λDefault for models in Experiment 1. We
test this by performing a model comparison across the two conditions for each LLM.
We obtain marginal likelihoods for two models: (1) a single λ parameter for LLM responses in both chain-of-thought and
default prompting (the null hypothesis); and (2) ordinal λ parameters for the two prompts, restricted to λChain of Thought >
λDefault (our hypothesis). Because this expands the parameter space combinatorially, we coarsen our grid to λ ∈ [0, 1] with
increments of .1, βS ∈ [1, 10] with increments of 1, and βL ∈ [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]. We report results in Table 1 in the main text.

Effects of CoT. We find that allowing LLMs to reason prior
to producing an utterance improves their helpfulness, but often at the cost of honesty (Fig. 2B, Table 2 in the Appendix
for full numeric results). The psychological model confirms this: CoT shifts the inferred utilities strongly towards
helpfulness (Fig. 2C). A model comparison testing if λ is
greater with chain-of-thought prompting provides extremely
strong evidence that this is the case in four of the seven
models tested: we compare results for a model assuming
λCoT > λDefault against a null model with λCoT = λDefault
and obtain Bayes factors exceeding 1 × 1015 ; see Table 1
and Appendix B for details.

However, these approaches often sidestep the nuances and
complexities of conversational language use (Kasirzadeh &
Gabriel, 2023), where these values don’t exist in isolation
and have to be traded off based on context. In this paper, we
use experimental paradigms from cognitive psychology that
tease these values apart and put them in conflict, and compare LLM behavior directly to analogous studies in humans.
This bridges studies of alignment in LLMs and communicative norms in people and follows in a long tradition of using
human communicative norms to understand (Ruis et al.,
2022; Sravanthi et al., 2024; Lipkin et al., 2023; Fried et al.,
2023) and improve (Dale & Reiter, 1995; Fried et al., 2018)
conversational agents. To our knowledge ours is the first to
test the ability of LLMs to make nuanced trade-offs between
honesty and helpfulness, and compare them to humans.

Chain of Thought versus Default prompting (Exp 1). Our hypothesis is that chain-of-thought prompting will bias models
towards helpfulness over honesty. Formally, this means that the λChain of Thought > λDefault for models in Experiment 1. We
test this by performing a model comparison across the two conditions for each LLM.
We obtain marginal likelihoods for two models: (1) a single λ parameter for LLM responses in both chain-of-thought and
default prompting (the null hypothesis); and (2) ordinal λ parameters for the two prompts, restricted to λChain of Thought >
λDefault (our hypothesis). Because this expands the parameter space combinatorially, we coarsen our grid to λ ∈ [0, 1] with
increments of .1, βS ∈ [1, 10] with increments of 1, and βL ∈ [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]. We report results in Table 1 in the main text.

C. Full Results Tables
We provide the tables containing the results of experiment 1 (Table 2), experiment 2 (Table 3), and experiment 3 (Table 4).
In Table 2, GPT-4 and GPT-4 turbo did not have a large enough proportion of lies for the ‘percentage of lies helpful’ metric
to be meaningful, thus the entries are left blank. In Table 3, the Llama 2 70B chat (denoted Llama2-RLHF) and Llama 2
70B (denoted Llama-2) models had some experiments where the responses were either uniformly “say the utterance” or
“stay silent”, and thus there was no space to perform a meaningful analysis and the entries are also left blank.

Figure 4. Visualizing the helpfulness-honesty trade-off in GPT-4 Turbo. Top row shows human participants from Sumers et al. (2023),
middle row shows GPT-4 Turbo in the mushroom setting (Exp 2), bottom shows GPT-4 Turbo in the housing setting (Exp 3). Left:
neutral prompt. Center: prompted to focus on honesty only. Right: prompted to focus on helpfulness only. Dots show individual trial
responses and lines show nonparametric regressions. With a neutral prompt, GPT-4 Turbo refuses to endorse false utterances regardless of
their helpfulness (Rows B and C, left column, blue lines). However, it is highly sensitive to the helpfulness of true utterances, endorsing
only when helpful (Rows B and C, left column, orange lines). Prompted for honesty only, it successfully adjusts in the Housing setting
(Row C, center) but not Mushrooms (Row B, center). Finally, prompted for helpfulness only, it is willing to endorse false utterances as
their helpfulness increases (Rows B and C, right column) — resembling humans’ default response (Row A, left column).

Thus, in our experiments, “truthfulness” and “supportedness”
are synonymous and can easily be measured (false claims
are not supported; true claims are). In contrast, we cannot
claim to know what an LLM “believes.” However, in GPT-4
Turbo at least, empirical results (Fig. 4) and reasoning traces
(Appendix D3, D4) clearly suggest that the model correctly
endorses which statements are true or false based on the
provided information – i.e., it “believes” this ground-truth
information about the world state. Thus, we chose to use the
term “honesty” to describe our work: it is consistent with our
formal model (unlike “supportedness”) — and intuitively,
an agent makes tradeoffs with respect to what they believe
to be true (which argues against “truthfulness”). Similarly,
there are many alternative formalizations of helpfulness: for
example, the Question Under Discussion (Roberts, 2012)
assumes that discourse is oriented towards answering a particular question at any point in time. Helpfulness is thus
measured by how much an utterance reduces the listener’s
uncertainty with respect to that question. This is a narrower
definition of helpfulness which is subsumed by the decisiontheoretic measure used here (see discussion in Sumers et al.,
2023), but it may be closer in spirit to Askell et al. (2021).

In this study, we formalized and studied how LLMs navigate
trade-offs between helpfulness and honesty. We used a controlled experimental paradigm from cognitive psychology
to compare LLMs to people, revealing and steering their implicit conversational values. Our contribution complements
benchmark-based evaluation (Srivastava et al., 2023; Liang
et al., 2023) by exploring how human values (Kasirzadeh &
Gabriel, 2023) manifest in LLMs. Of course, the methods
we borrow from cognitive science possess inherent limitations: The controlled domains we use provide precision,
but cannot guarantee generalization to real-world contexts.
This, however, is the same challenge faced by all human
experiments. Perhaps more concerningly, while human comparisons are crucial to understand LLMs as conversational
agents, we acknowledge that people necessarily bring vastly
different social and physical groundings (Lampinen, 2022;
Shanahan, 2024), making all such comparisons fraught.
Formalizing honesty and helpfulness presents its own challenges. Evans et al. (2021) define LLM honesty as the model
saying things that it “believes” – in contrast to LLM truthfulness, which they define as the model saying things that are
actually true. Finally, Menick et al. (2022) define a related
notion, supportedness, as saying things that are supported by
evidence. Our work touches on all of these concepts. In our
formal model, Eq. 2 implements “truthfulness” (accuracy
with respect to the true world state). However, the RSA
framework (Goodman & Frank, 2016; Frank & Goodman,
2012) assumes that the speaker has direct access to the true
world state — thus, in our model, “honesty” and “truthfulness” are equivalent and “supportedness” is not meaningful.
Our experimental paradigm (Section 4) prompts the LLM
with the true state of the world (the mushroom information).
